svg.title: Multicast failures are silent: five observation layers and the only evidence that actually proves delivery
svg.desc: Left: the reason failures are invisible - there is no ICMP unreachable because the packet is valid, no syslog because nothing errors, no retransmission because the transport is UDP, so the only trace is a missing packet at the far end. Right: a five-layer stack of evidence, from the application down: RTP or MPEG loss and jitter from the receiver, interface and queue counters on the path, mroute state and packet counts in the control plane, hardware replication entries in the data plane, and the IGMP snooping table at Layer 2. A bottom band lists the three active tests that beat passive monitoring: a synthetic join from a probe in every segment, mtrace from receiver to source, and a scheduled egress counter collection at peak.
svg.text: Nothing reports a multicast failure. Everything must be observed.
Unicast breaks loudly and multicast breaks quietly: the packet is valid IPv4 and the protocol has no error path.
WHY NOTHING TELLS YOU
No ICMP unreachable
The packet is well formed and the group is
routable. There is simply no tree, so it is
dropped at the RPF check.
No syslog, no SNMP trap
Dropping a multicast packet is normal
operation, not an error condition worth
a log entry. Nobody can alert on it.
No retransmission
UDP has no recovery. The encoder keeps
sending into a tree that no longer exists.
FIVE LAYERS OF EVIDENCE, TOP DOWN
5 Application RTP/MPEG loss, jitter, MOS, frozen picture counter
4 Transport interface counters, queue drops, policer drops
3 Control plane (S,G) exists, RPF correct, OIL correct, packet count rising
2 Data plane hardware entry present, replication slots free, TCAM count
1 Layer 2 snooping group entry, mrouter port, querier alive
Each layer can be green while the one below fails. That is the whole problem.
THREE ACTIVE TESTS THAT BEAT PASSIVE MONITORING
Synthetic join per segment
A probe in every VLAN joins the channel
and reports loss. It is the only way to
know a small segment is broken.
join -> 5 s of RTP -> loss % -> alert
mtrace end to end
Walks the actual tree hop by hop and
reports where the last packet was seen.
The only tool that shows the path, not
the intention.
Peak-hour counters
Collect egress byte and packet counters
at the busiest 15 minutes, not at 09:00
when only four people are watching.
Two numbers per hop: what should leave,
what did leave.
Write the observation plan into the design: which layer, which command, which threshold, who is paged. Silent failures only stay small when monitoring is designed before the rollout.
